opening.headline: Understanding why splitting agents into multiple parts results in slower performance and higher costs, and establishing criteria to determine when splitting is beneficial.
body: Breaking agents down by role makes the structure appear neat. However, as the number of agents increases, the number of calls and messages required for coordination grows, and token costs rise significantly. According to Anthropic's data, agents consume about four times as many tokens as a chat, while multi-agent systems consume about fifteen times as many.

In this course, we follow Anthropic's multi-agent research system architecture and compare the differences between handoff mechanisms that transfer control versus sub-agents that return only results. We then examine the case where the benefits of context isolation and parallel exploration exceed their associated costs.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain handoff, subagent, and multi-agent research structures
Can determine conditions under which multi-agent is beneficial

screens.title: A structure where agents become slower and more expensive as their number increases
screens.lead: Increasing the agent leads to a slower system and higher costs. Let's examine the situation below and think about where the costs are being incurred.

visual.alt: Bar chart comparing relative token usage of chat, single-agent, and multi-agent.

paragraphs: Splitting one agent's work among multiple agents creates new dynamics. It involves coordination where agents explain their tasks to each other, receive results, combine them, and avoid duplication. This coordination relies on calls and tokens. Anthropic explains that their agents use about four times as many tokens as chat, and multi-agent systems use about fifteen times as many tokens as chat.

Cost is not the only issue. In early research systems, there were errors such as spawning as many as 50 sub-agents for a simple query. There were also instances of endlessly searching for non-existent sources or sending unnecessary updates to one another. As the number of agents increases, the complexity of coordination grows rapidly.

Then, in what cases does the division side benefit? This is the question raised in this lesson, and the answer lies in whether parallelism and context separation are required. Let us first review your own experiences.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: The decision to add another agent is not the decision to add another function, but the decision to bear one more tuning cost.

screens.outro: Let's recall why we decided to divide it.

screens.title: Think about why the reason for splitting into multiple agents.
screens.lead: After first thinking through the question mentally and making a choice, the instructor's thought process is revealed. Answers are not entered or submitted.

items.prompt: Why was the agent divided into multiple parts?
items.answer: If the reason is simply "it looks well-structured," it warrants further examination. Valid reasons for splitting typically involve two cases: when multiple independent tasks need to be executed concurrently, or when it's impractical to include all information within the context of a single agent.

items.prompt: Has any agent ever been problematic because it holds all information within a single context?
items.answer: As the number of documents encountered during investigation grows, important instructions are often obscured. In such cases, delegating only the exploration phase to a separate agent while retrieving only the conclusion ensures the main context remains cleanly preserved.

items.prompt: Can you distinguish what you gained from what you lost after splitting it?
items.answer: The gains are parallelism and context separation, role-based instructions and tool limitations. The losses include token costs, tuning complexity, and the difficulty of agents sharing information. This course's approach is to evaluate these two aspects side by side.

screens.outro: I will verify the structure by checking how the actual system divides and combines components.

screens.title: Research System Architecture: Lead and Sub-agents
screens.lead: Follow the step-by-step process of Anthropic's multi-agent research system as it handles a query. Select the right arrow to view the next step.

visual.alt: This is a structure where the lead agent formulates a plan, subordinate agents conduct parallel searches, and the results are passed through the citation agent.
labels: Summarize only the core points and return them.

steps.title: 1. Query Analysis and Strategy
steps.body: When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes the query and establishes an access strategy. This architecture follows the orchestrator-worker pattern, where the lead coordinates and specialized subordinate agents operate in parallel.

steps.title: 2. Store the plan in memory
steps.body: Lee stores the plan in memory. Since the context exceeds 200,000 tokens, it gets truncated; therefore, information that must persist like the plan is preserved outside the context.

steps.title: 3. Sub-agent Generation
steps.body: Lee creates specialized subordinate agents with specific investigation tasks. There is no fixed number of such agents to create. Each subordinate agent requires a goal, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and defined operational boundaries. Ambiguous descriptions can lead to redundant searches or gaps in coverage.

steps.title: 4. Search and evaluate individually
steps.body: Sub-agents independently perform web searches and evaluate tool results. Each agent simultaneously explores different aspects within its own context window and returns only the most important tokens to the lead. The essence of searching is compression, as described in the document's explanation.

steps.title: 5. Comprehensive and Additional Investigation Judgment
steps.body: Read evaluates the received results to determine whether further investigation is needed. If insufficient, it creates additional subordinate agents or refines its strategy. If sufficient, it exits the investigation loop.

steps.title: 6. Return after citation to the user
steps.body: Once sufficient information is available, the citation agent processes documents and reports to attach source locations that correspond to each claim. The final result, with all claims linked to sources, is returned to the user. The scale of effort should match the complexity of the query; it is stated that a single agent making 3 to 10 tool calls is sufficient for simple fact verification tasks.

screens.outro: Now that we've examined the structure, I'll compare the two methods regarding how control authority is transferred.

screens.title: Handoff and Sub-agent: Where is the authority located?
screens.lead: Compare how control and final response ownership differ by alternately selecting between two states.

visual.alt: A diagram comparing two structures: in handoff, control shifts to an expert, and in subordinate agents, control returns to an administrator.
labels: The final response is written by the administrator.

states.label: handoff
states.body: Handoff is a mechanism where a specialist agent receives the conversation and response flow of a specific branch. According to OpenAI documentation, handoff is most appropriate when the expert is not merely providing assistance but should become the owner of the next response. In the Agents SDK, handoff is represented as a tool and takes the default name in the form of `transfer_to_<agent_name>`. For example, if a classification agent receives a list such as `handoffs=[billing_agent, handoff(refund_agent)]`, the model calls the appropriate branch as a tool and transfers control. Each expert's scope is kept narrow, and the handoff explanation is kept short and specific.

states.label: subagent
states.body: A subordinate agent is a separate agent launched by the main agent to take on specific subtasks. In OpenAI's documentation, this corresponds to a manager maintaining ownership of the final response while delegating an expert to perform tasks with limited capabilities. According to the Claude Agent SDK documentation, a subordinate agent operates within its own dialogue, performs intermediate tool calls and retains the results internally, and only sends the final message back to its parent. The parent receives only a concise summary of all files read by the subordinate agent, not the full files themselves. Independent tasks can run in parallel, and each subordinate agent can be given dedicated instructions and a limited set of tools.

screens.outro: Now we summarize the benefits and costs of separation in one glance.

Independent tasks are executed in parallel: It ends at the slowest one time.. You can reduce Dedicated guidelines and limited tools per subordinate agent. However, multi-agent systems use chat context: Approximately 15x token. All agents must share the same context or This does not suit work that involves heavy mutual dependency..

marks.span: Intermediate tool results are only summarized and do not accumulate in the main conversation.
marks.note: The benefit of context isolation. Even if subordinate agents read dozens of files, only a concise summary remains in the main context, preventing contamination of the main context.

marks.span: It ends at the slowest one time.
marks.note: The advantage of parallel search is that when performed sequentially, the times add up, but when performed in parallel, the total time is reduced to the longest single time.
The benefits of role separation. For example, you can grant only read tools to subordinate agents used for document review, preventing accidental file modifications.
This is the highest cost. It must be high enough to cover the increased cost associated with the work's value in order to be economically viable.

marks.span: This does not suit work that involves heavy mutual dependency.
marks.note: This condition is invalid. The document explains that coding tasks are often less likely to be divided in parallel compared to research tasks.

screens.outro: Let's apply this standard to a practical example.

screens.title: Explanation: When lower agents are deployed due to context isolation
screens.lead: The instructor explains step by step why subordinate agents are deployed when investigating the entire repository. Select the right arrow to proceed.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: A request was made to the main agent: "Please summarize how the authentication flow works in this repository." If the main agent directly reads the repository, dozens of file contents fill the main context. However, when it's time to summarize, important instructions and requests are buried among the file contents.

steps.title: Stage 1: Agent per module
steps.body: The main component spawns three subordinate agents per module, each responsible for authentication, session, and authorization modules. The subordinate agents start fresh in each conversation and thus are unaffected by the content of other agents, reading only their own module's data.

steps.title: Step 2: Return only the summary
steps.body: Each subordinate agent reads files, searches, and builds context. However, intermediate tool calls and their results remain within the subordinate agent, and only the final discovery summary is returned to the parent. Regardless of how many files each subordinate agent reads, only the summary is sent back to the main agent.

steps.title: Step 3: Focus main on synthesis
steps.body: There remain only three summaries in the main context. Since the main context has no reading context, it focuses on connecting the three summaries to clarify the authentication flow. The main context remains accurate and concise.

steps.title: Step 4: Parallelism and Cost
steps.body: The three sub-agents can run concurrently, so the total execution time is closer to that of the slowest single agent rather than the sum of sequential execution times. Conversely, the total token budget increases. Each sub-agent accumulates its own context, and the main agent also consumes tokens for coordination and synthesis.

steps.title: Step 5: Required Tuning
steps.body: This architecture works well only if the main agent clearly communicates to each subordinate agent the goal, output format, and operational boundaries. Without such boundaries, the three subordinate agents may end up reading the same file, leading to redundancy. The research system has also mentioned that it repeatedly performed the same search due to ambiguous instructions.

steps.title: Step 6: Design of Sub-agents
steps.body: Sub-agents define their name, description, prompt, and tools used within the code. The description serves as the basis for determining when the main agent should invoke this sub-agent. In this example, the module investigation sub-agent is safely given only read and search tools, without providing tools that modify files. Limiting the available tools prevents accidental code modifications during exploration. Nesting sub-agents to delegate larger tasks back to other sub-agents should be avoided; instead, limiting the depth to one level makes the process easier to trace. At the same time, the arrival order of results may not be guaranteed.

steps.title: Instructor's judgment
steps.body: This structure is valid because the reasons for separation—context protection and parallelism—are clearly distinct. Conversely, if the same structure is applied to a scenario involving only a single file modification, there are no independent tasks to parallelize, and token usage simply increases unnecessarily. If the reasons for separation cannot be expressed in a single sentence, it is safer to start with a single agent.

screens.outro: I will conclude with a single sentence as the criterion.

screens.title: Key Takeaway: You must be able to explain why division is necessary.
screens.lead: We consolidate the criterion for deciding whether to use multi-agent systems.

paragraphs: Multi-agent systems should only be used when parallelism and context isolation are required. Parallelism enables multiple independent investigation directions to proceed simultaneously, reducing overall time, while context isolation ensures that intermediate exploration content does not accumulate in the main conversation. These benefits are particularly significant in broad, exploratory tasks where multiple directions are investigated concurrently.

You should also remember the difference between these two approaches. Handoff transfers control to an expert who then takes responsibility for the next response. A subordinate agent receives the response from the main agent and returns the result. In either case, each agent's responsibilities are kept narrow, and instructions, tools, or policies are only shared when they actually change.

We also calculate the cost. Multi-agent systems consume approximately 15 times more tokens than chat, so the value of the task must exceed this cost. Tasks where all agents share the same context or have high interdependence, or where parallelization is limited—such as most coding tasks—tend to be better served by a single agent. Conversely, tasks involving broad information gathering, vast amounts of data that cannot fit into a single context, or complex interactions with multiple tools benefit significantly from separation. Anthropic explains that multi-agent systems excel in tasks that are both high-value and highly parallelizable. If the reasons for separation cannot be captured in one sentence, start with one.

Finally, if we decide to divide responsibilities, we must design the tuning. Clearly specify each subordinate agent's goals, output format, and operational boundaries, and determine the number of agents based on the complexity of the query. Simply adding multiple agents for straightforward fact verification only increases costs.

The way to apply this standard in actual design meetings is simple. When a proposal to add an agent is made, the agent is asked in one sentence whether it addresses concurrency, context separation, or separation of instructions and tools. If none of these apply, then the proposal merely complicates the architecture. If there is a reason, estimate whether the benefit associated with that reason exceeds the corresponding token cost, and if the estimation is difficult, first compare it on a small scale.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Sharing is not the default. It is an exception to be chosen only when there are valid reasons such as parallelism or context separation.

glossary.def: This is a method where one agent forwards the conversation to a specialized agent, who then takes responsibility for responding.
The main agent launches a separate agent to handle a specific portion of work, which operates within its own context and returns the results.
This results in the effect where only a summary is transmitted to the main context, and the intermediate exploration content of the subordinate agent is not accumulated.
It involves multiple agents simultaneously conducting independent investigation directions.
It is a central agent that plans in the research system and creates subordinate agents to aggregate results.

misconceptions.myth: The more agents there are, the smarter they become.
misconceptions.fact: As the number of agents increases, the complexity of orchestration and token costs also rise. There have been actual instances where excessive sub-agents were spawned for simple queries.

misconceptions.myth: Sub-agents are beneficial for all tasks.
misconceptions.fact: This is not suitable for tasks that have high interdependence or share the same context. Tasks with limited parallelization opportunities yield little benefit.

misconceptions.myth: Handoff and subordinate agents are identical in method, differing only in name.
misconceptions.fact: Handoff transfers control to an expert, while subordinate agents receive only the result, keeping the main agent in possession of the response. The owner of the final response is different.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Multi-agent systems should only be used when parallelism and context isolation are required.
Handoff involves transferring control, and the subordinate agent returns a summary.
Multi-agent systems require significant token usage, so the value of the work must exceed the cost.
If the reason for separation cannot be stated, begin with a single agent.
